In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of vaccines against hepatitis B virus (HBV) and the rodent hepaciviruses, the woodchuck hepatitis virus (WHV) and the ground squirrel hepatitis virus (GSHV), using the viral core proteins as vaccine carrier platforms.
the development of a novel vaccine platform for the prevention of hepatitis B virus infections in humans.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rodent core protein WHcAg is a more immunogenic and more versatile vaccine carrier platform than the human core protein HBcAg.
WHcAg is a better antigen and immunogen than HBcAg, at least in the mouse.
the rodent hepaciviruses are not “just another” rodent model for HBV infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rodent core protein antigens are as immunogenic as HBcAg and that WHcAg may be the most suitable antigen for use in human vaccination.
the rodent hepa-dnavirus core proteins are equal or superior to HBcAg at every level tested and that WHcAg appears to be the most suitable hepadnavirus-derived core protein for vaccine development.
the rodent core protein WHcAg is the best of the three rodent core proteins tested for vaccine carrier use and that WHcAg is a good candidate for vaccine development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rodent core protein, WHcAg, may be a better candidate than HBcAg for the development of a human hepadnavirus vaccine carrier platform.
the rodent hepacivirus core proteins are as immunogenic as HBcAg at both the B-cell and the T-cell levels.
